Sweatt v. Painter. In 1950, Heman Sweatt was denied admission to the University of Texas Law School solely on grounds of race. Rather than admit him, Texas hastily created a separate law school for him. The Supreme Court voted unanimously against Texas.

Chief Justice Fred Vinson found the new school patently unequal in every respect that mattered. It had inferior physical facilities, a smaller faculty, a limited library, and lacked the prestige of the University of Texas. Vinson wrote that the separate facilities were inherently unequal in educational quality and prestige. This was a finding easy for courts to verify and replicate.

The decision did not explicitly overrule Plessy v. Ferguson, but it applied the equal part of separate but equal so stringently that true separation became legally impossible. Sweatt's case demonstrated the practical futility of separate but equal in graduate and professional education, where intangible factors like prestige matter tremendously.

This case was part of the NAACP's strategic litigation campaign that would culminate in Brown v. Board of Education four years later. Thurgood Marshall argued Sweatt before the Supreme Court. Sweatt preceded another 1950 decision, McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents, which also stripped away Plessy's foundation. By the time Brown arrived in 1954, the court system had already been prepared to recognize that the separate but equal doctrine could not survive scrutiny, at least not in education.
